decks.title: Atmospheric and Environmental Chemistry — Part 1: Acid rain and global warming
goals: Write equations showing how oxides of sulphur and nitrogen make acids in rainwater, and describe the effects of acid rain
Name the main greenhouse gases and their sources
Suggest measures that reduce emissions of greenhouse gases and the gases that cause acid rain

slides.heading: Air, Rain and a Warming World
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how burning fuels changes the rain and the climate.

visual.alt: Flow: burning fuels, gases in the air, acid rain and global warming

slides.narration: Every car, power station and furnace sends gases into the air. Some of these gases turn rain acidic. Others trap heat and warm the planet. This part follows both stories, from the chimney to the consequences.

slides.heading: Where the gases come from

rows: Burning coal and oil that contain sulphur; roasting sulphide ores; refineries
Petrol and diesel engines; furnaces and power stations at very high temperature

visual.alt: Table of sources of sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides

slides.narration: Sulphur dioxide comes mainly from burning coal and oil that contain sulphur, and from refining and roasting ores. Nitrogen oxides come from the very hot flames in engines and furnaces, where nitrogen and oxygen of the air combine. Volcanoes and lightning add some naturally.

slides.heading: Sulphur oxides: from fuel to acid
slides.body_md: Burning sulphur in fuel gives **sulphur dioxide**, which reacts with water to give **sulphurous acid**. Some is oxidised in the air to **sulphur trioxide**, which gives **sulphuric acid**.

visual.alt: Table of four equations from sulphur to sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Sulphur in fuel burns to form sulphur dioxide. In the damp air it dissolves to give sulphurous acid. Some sulphur dioxide is oxidised to sulphur trioxide, and that dissolves in water to give sulphuric acid, a strong acid.

slides.heading: How acid rain forms and where it falls
slides.body_md: Follow the gases from the chimney to the cloud and down to soil and lake.

slides.narration: Smoke and exhaust carry sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide upward. In a cloud they dissolve in the water droplets and form acids. When the rain falls, it carries the acids to soil, trees, rivers and lakes, and to buildings.

slides.heading: Quick check: sulphuric acid
slides.body_md: Which equation shows the formation of sulphuric acid from sulphur trioxide?
slides.narration: Sulphur trioxide must react with water.

slides.heading: Nitrogen oxides: from air to nitric acid
slides.body_md: In very hot engines and furnaces, nitrogen and oxygen of the air combine. **Nitric oxide** is oxidised to **nitrogen dioxide**, which dissolves in water and oxygen to give **nitric acid**.

visual.alt: Table of three equations from nitrogen to nitric acid

slides.narration: Nitrogen and oxygen do not react at normal temperatures, but in a very hot engine they form nitric oxide. In air this becomes nitrogen dioxide, a brown gas. Nitrogen dioxide, with oxygen and rainwater, gives nitric acid.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: following the nitrogen
slides.body_md: Show that each step that turns nitrogen of the air into nitric acid is balanced.
bullets: Step 1: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO: 2 nitrogen and 2 oxygen atoms on each side.
Step 2: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂: 2 nitrogen and 4 oxygen atoms on each side.
Step 3: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃: 4 nitrogen, 12 oxygen and 4 hydrogen atoms on each side.
Check the masses of step 3: the left side totals 252 and the right side 252.

visual.alt: Flow: nitrogen, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, nitric acid

slides.narration: Count atoms in each step. In the first, two nitrogen and two oxygen atoms appear on both sides. In the second, two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms. In the third, four nitrogen, twelve oxygen and four hydrogen atoms. All three balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: nitric acid
slides.body_md: The brown gas that dissolves in rainwater to form nitric acid is…
slides.narration: Which oxide of nitrogen is brown?

slides.heading: Effects of acid rain

rows: Washes out nutrients such as calcium and magnesium; harms plants and soil organisms
Water becomes too acidic for fish eggs, fish and many water plants
Marble and limestone are eaten away: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂

visual.alt: Table of the effects of acid rain on soil, water and buildings

slides.narration: Acid rain washes nutrients from the soil and weakens trees and crops. In lakes it makes the water too acidic for fish and plants. It also attacks marble and limestone, because calcium carbonate reacts with the acids, so statues and monuments lose their surface.

slides.heading: Reducing acid rain

visual.alt: Flow of ways to reduce acid rain

slides.narration: To stop acid rain, cut the gases at the source. Use fuels with less sulphur, remove sulphur dioxide from chimney gases, fit catalytic converters to vehicles, and use cleaner sources of energy. As of 2026, India supplies petrol and diesel under the Bharat Stage six standard, which has very low sulphur.

slides.narration: Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground. The ground gives out heat as infrared radiation. Some of it escapes to space, but greenhouse gases absorb part of it and send it back down. This natural effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life.

slides.heading: Greenhouse gases and their sources

rows: Evaporation from oceans, lakes and plants
Burning fossil fuels, cement making, clearing forests
Wetlands, cattle, coal mining, leaks of natural gas, waste dumps
Fertilised farmland, burning fuels, vehicle engines

visual.alt: Table of greenhouse gases and their sources

slides.narration: The main greenhouse gases are water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and oxides of nitrogen. Water vapour comes from evaporation. Carbon dioxide comes mostly from burning fossil fuels and clearing forests. Methane comes from wetlands, cattle and coal mines, and nitrogen oxides from fertilisers and fuels.

slides.heading: Quick check: a source
slides.body_md: Burning coal in a power station mainly adds which greenhouse gas to the air?
slides.narration: Coal is mostly carbon.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a rise in carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: The carbon dioxide at a busy roadside was 400 parts per million before a new flyover opened and 460 parts per million after. (Imagined readings.) Find the percentage rise.
bullets: Step 1: rise = 460 − 400 = 60 parts per million.
Step 2: percentage rise = 60 ÷ 400 × 100 = **15%**.
Step 3: the extra gas came mostly from vehicles burning fuel: C + O₂ → CO₂ (carbon from the fuel).

visual.alt: Worked table of roadside carbon dioxide before and after

slides.narration: Subtract the first reading from the second to get the rise, which is sixty parts per million. Divide the rise by the first reading and multiply by one hundred. The rise is fifteen per cent. The extra carbon dioxide comes from fuel burning in vehicles.

slides.heading: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions

nodes.label: Save energy at home and in industry
Use solar, wind and hydro power
Use public transport and share journeys

visual.alt: Flow of measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions

slides.narration: To limit warming, use less energy, switch to solar, wind and hydro power, share journeys or use public transport, plant trees and protect forests, and manage waste and fertilisers so that less methane and nitrous oxide escape.

slides.body_md: True or false: planting trees helps to reduce the carbon dioxide in the air.
slides.narration: What do green plants take in for photosynthesis?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from fuels dissolve in rain to make sulphurous, sulphuric and nitric acids.
Acid rain harms soil, lakes and marble buildings.
Greenhouse gases (water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, oxides of nitrogen) trap heat and cause global warming.
Fewer fossil fuels, cleaner energy, trees and better waste management reduce both problems.

rows: Fuels containing sulphur; hot engines and furnaces
Fossil fuels, forest clearing, farming and waste

visual.alt: Summary table of acid rain and global warming

slides.narration: To recap. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain, which harms soil, water and buildings. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat and warm the planet. Cleaner fuels and energy, more trees and better waste management help with both.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **balanced** equations and name each acid: sulphurous, sulphuric, nitric.
Give **two effects** of acid rain on soil and on aquatic life.
Link each greenhouse gas with a **source** and a way to **reduce** it.
Do not confuse the **greenhouse effect** (heat trapping) with the **ozone hole** (ultraviolet).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Balance every equation and name the acids. Give effects on soil and on aquatic life. Match each greenhouse gas with a source and a remedy. And do not mix up the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole, which is a different problem.

goals: Write equations for the formation of ozone and explain the role of the ozone layer
Name the chemicals that deplete the ozone layer
Explain why dissolved oxygen and minerals matter, and how heavy metals, plastics, sewage and pesticides harm water bodies

slides.heading: The Ozone Layer and Our Water
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a shield high above us, and the substances in water that help or harm.

visual.alt: Flow: ozone layer, dissolved substances, pollutants

slides.narration: High above us, a thin layer of ozone shields life from harmful sunlight. Down below, water carries oxygen and minerals that life needs, and sometimes poisons that it does not. This part covers both.

slides.heading: The ozone layer in the atmosphere
slides.body_md: Most ozone lies in a band inside the **stratosphere**. It absorbs **harmful ultraviolet radiation** while visible light passes through.

slides.narration: The stratosphere sits above the layer of air where we live. Inside it is a band rich in ozone. This band absorbs the most harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun, while ordinary light reaches the ground.

slides.heading: How ozone is formed
slides.body_md: In the upper atmosphere, **ultraviolet radiation** splits oxygen molecules into atoms. An atom joins a molecule of oxygen to form **ozone**.

visual.alt: Table of the equations for the formation of ozone

slides.narration: Ultraviolet radiation splits an oxygen molecule into two oxygen atoms. Each atom then joins an oxygen molecule to make a molecule of ozone, which has three atoms. Overall, three molecules of oxygen make two of ozone.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting atoms in ozone formation
slides.body_md: Show that the overall equation for ozone formation balances.
bullets: Step 1: ultraviolet radiation splits one oxygen molecule into two atoms: $\ce{O2 ->[UV] 2O}$.
Step 2: each atom joins a further oxygen molecule: $\ce{O + O2 -> O3}$, twice over, using two more molecules of oxygen.
Step 3: add up: three molecules of oxygen (6 atoms) give two molecules of ozone (6 atoms), so **3O₂ → 2O₃**.
Check the masses: 3 × 32 = 96; 2 × 48 = 96.

visual.alt: Overall equation: three oxygen molecules give two ozone molecules
visual.caption: Overall change; ultraviolet energy is needed

slides.narration: Count oxygen atoms. Three molecules of oxygen contain six atoms. Two molecules of ozone also contain six atoms, so the equation balances. The masses also match at ninety six on each side.

slides.heading: Quick check: forming ozone
slides.body_md: Which equation shows an oxygen atom joining an oxygen molecule to form ozone?
slides.narration: Ozone has three oxygen atoms.

slides.heading: Why the ozone layer matters

headers: Without enough ozone, more ultraviolet reaches the ground
rows: More skin cancer and eye cataracts
Damage to tiny plankton that feed other life

visual.alt: Table of effects of extra ultraviolet radiation

slides.narration: The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays. If it thins, more rays reach the ground, causing skin cancer and eye cataracts in people, damage to crops, and harm to the tiny plankton that feed life in the oceans.

slides.heading: What damages the ozone layer
slides.body_md: Certain man-made chemicals rise to the stratosphere and **destroy ozone faster than it is made**. Only their **names** are needed at this level.

rows: Refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays, foam

visual.alt: Table of ozone-depleting chemicals and their former uses

slides.narration: The main ozone-depleting chemicals are chlorofluorocarbons, halons, carbon tetrachloride and methyl bromide. They were used in refrigeration, sprays, fire extinguishers, cleaning and farming. Under an international agreement, their use has been phased out, and as of 2026 the ozone layer is slowly recovering.

slides.heading: Quick check: the shield
slides.body_md: The ozone layer is important to living things because it…
slides.narration: Think about which radiation it removes.

slides.heading: Dissolved oxygen and minerals in water

rows: Fish and other water animals breathe it; bacteria use it to break down wastes
Water plants use it in photosynthesis
Keep body fluids balanced and help nerves work

visual.alt: Table of dissolved substances in natural water and why each is needed

slides.narration: Natural water is not just water. Dissolved oxygen lets fish breathe. Dissolved carbon dioxide feeds water plants. Calcium and magnesium build bones, teeth and shells. Sodium and potassium keep body fluids balanced. Small amounts of nitrates and phosphates feed plants.

slides.heading: Warm water holds less oxygen
slides.body_md: The amount of oxygen that water can hold **falls as the temperature rises**.

y.label: Dissolved oxygen at saturation (mg per litre)

visual.alt: Graph of the oxygen that water can hold against its temperature: a falling line from about fourteen at zero degrees to about six and a half at forty degrees
visual.caption: Approximate textbook values for fresh water in contact with air at sea-level pressure; books differ slightly.

slides.narration: Cold water can hold much more oxygen than warm water. At zero degrees, fresh water can hold about fourteen milligrams per litre, but at thirty degrees only about seven and a half. This is why fish suffer in hot, still water.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: oxygen in a pond
slides.body_md: A pond holds 5000 litres of water with 6 mg of dissolved oxygen per litre. (Imagined figures.) Find the mass of dissolved oxygen in grams.
bullets: Step 1: total in mg = 6 × 5000 = 30000 mg.
Step 3: this is a tiny fraction of the water, but it is enough for fish and bacteria to survive.

visual.alt: Worked table for the oxygen in a pond

slides.narration: Multiply the oxygen in each litre by the number of litres to get thirty thousand milligrams. Then divide by one thousand to change to grams. The pond holds thirty grams of dissolved oxygen.

slides.heading: Quick check: dissolved oxygen
slides.body_md: On a hot, still day fish in a shallow pond come to the surface gasping because…
slides.narration: Remember what temperature does to dissolved gases.

slides.heading: A toxic heavy metal: Minamata disease
slides.body_md: A factory at Minamata Bay in Japan discharged waste containing **mercury**. Microbes changed it to **methylmercury**, which built up along the food chain and poisoned people who ate the fish.

nodes.label: Plankton and small fish absorb it

visual.alt: Flow showing how mercury reached people through the food chain at Minamata

slides.narration: Minamata disease was first recognised in the nineteen fifties in Japan. Mercury from a factory entered the bay. Microbes turned it into methylmercury, which built up in fish and shellfish. People who ate them suffered numbness, loss of coordination and damage to speech, sight and hearing. As of 2026, an international treaty controls mercury.

slides.heading: Plastics, sewage and pesticides

rows: Do not rot; block drains; animals swallow or get tangled in them; break into tiny pieces
Carries disease germs; adds nutrients that cause algae to bloom; bacteria then use up the dissolved oxygen
Wash in from fields; poison fish and other animals; build up along food chains

visual.alt: Table of the effects of plastics, sewage and pesticides on water bodies

slides.narration: Plastics do not rot, so they block drains and harm animals that swallow them. Untreated sewage carries germs and feeds algae. When the algae die, bacteria use up dissolved oxygen and fish die. Pesticides washed from fields poison water life and build up in food chains.

slides.heading: Sewage and the loss of oxygen

visual.alt: Flow showing how sewage and fertiliser run-off lead to the loss of dissolved oxygen

slides.narration: Sewage and fertiliser run-off add nutrients to a lake. Algae grow quickly and cover the surface. When they die, bacteria decay them and use up the dissolved oxygen. Without oxygen, fish and other animals die.

slides.heading: Quick check: Minamata
slides.body_md: Minamata disease was caused by compounds of which toxic metal?
slides.narration: The metal is a liquid at room temperature.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ozone forms from oxygen under ultraviolet radiation: O₂ → O + O, then O + O₂ → O₃. It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Chlorofluorocarbons, halons, carbon tetrachloride and methyl bromide deplete it.
Dissolved oxygen and minerals are essential in water; warm water holds less oxygen.
Mercury (Minamata disease), plastics, sewage and pesticides harm water life and people.

rows: Needed by fish; falls as water warms or is polluted
Builds up in the food chain

visual.alt: Summary table of the ozone layer and water pollution

slides.narration: To recap. Ozone forms from oxygen and shields us from ultraviolet radiation. Chlorofluorocarbons and similar chemicals damage it. Water needs dissolved oxygen and minerals. Mercury, plastics, sewage and pesticides pollute water and harm living things.

sections.heading: 1. Acid rain
sections.body_md:
**Acid rain** is rain that is more acidic than normal rain (normal rain is slightly acidic because of dissolved carbon dioxide). It forms when **oxides of sulphur and nitrogen** dissolve in the water droplets of clouds.

**Sources.** Sulphur dioxide: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil) that contain sulphur; roasting sulphide ores; volcanoes. Oxides of nitrogen: the very high temperature inside petrol and diesel engines, furnaces and power stations, where nitrogen and oxygen of the air combine; also lightning.

**Equations (oxides of sulphur):**
- $\ce{S + O2 -> SO2}$
- $\ce{SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3}$ (sulphurous acid)
- $\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$ (oxidation in air, helped by dust and other pollutants)
- $\ce{SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4}$ (sulphuric acid)

**Equations (oxides of nitrogen):**
- $\ce{N2 + O2 ->[\text{very high temperature}] 2NO}$
- $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ (brown gas)
- $\ce{4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O -> 4HNO3}$ (nitric acid). Some books write $\ce{3NO2 + H2O -> 2HNO3 + NO}$ instead; both are accepted.

**Effects.** *Soil:* washes out nutrients such as calcium and magnesium, harms plants and soil organisms. *Water bodies:* lakes and rivers become too acidic for fish eggs, fish and many water plants. *Buildings:* marble and limestone are attacked, for example $\ce{CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + H2O + CO2}$.

**Reducing acid rain:** fuels with less sulphur (as of 2026, Indian petrol and diesel meet the very low sulphur limits of Bharat Stage VI), removing sulphur dioxide from chimney gases, catalytic converters in vehicles, and cleaner energy.

sections.heading: 2. Global warming: greenhouse gases and their sources
sections.body_md:
The **greenhouse effect**: sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground. The ground gives out heat as **infrared radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** absorb part of it and send some back to the ground, so the Earth is warmer than it would be without them. This natural effect makes life possible. **Global warming** is the extra warming caused by human activities that increase these gases.

| Greenhouse gas | Chief sources |
|---|---|
| Water vapour | Evaporation from oceans, lakes and plants |
| Carbon dioxide | Burning fossil fuels, cement making, clearing forests, respiration and decay |
| Methane | Wetlands, cattle and other grazing animals, coal mining, leaks from natural gas supplies, waste dumps |
| Oxides of nitrogen (nitrous oxide) | Fertilised farmland, burning fuels, vehicle engines |

Burning carbon in fuel: $\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}$. Making cement from limestone: $\ce{CaCO3 ->[\Delta] CaO + CO2}$.

**Measures to reduce emissions:** save energy; use solar, wind and hydro power; use public transport and share journeys; plant trees and stop clearing forests; reduce waste and manage fertiliser and manure use.

**Time-sensitive points (as of 2026):** the carbon dioxide level in the air is above 420 parts per million, compared with about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution; the average surface temperature of the Earth has risen by roughly 1.2 °C or more since the late 1800s. Figures change every year; check the latest scientific reports.

key_terms.definition_md: A gas that absorbs infrared radiation from the ground and sends part of it back, warming the Earth.
The rise in the average temperature of the Earth caused by increased greenhouse gases.

sections.heading: 3. The ozone layer
sections.body_md:
**Ozone** ($\ce{O3}$) is a form of oxygen with three atoms in each molecule. Most of it lies in a band inside the **stratosphere**.

**Formation** (in the upper atmosphere, with ultraviolet radiation):
- $\ce{O2 ->[UV] 2O}$ (oxygen molecules are split into atoms)
- $\ce{O + O2 -> O3}$ (an atom joins an oxygen molecule)
- overall: $\ce{3O2 -> 2O3}$

**Function:** it absorbs the harmful **ultraviolet radiation** of the Sun, so less reaches the ground. Without it there would be more skin cancer and eye cataracts, damage to crops, and harm to plankton.

**Depletion by named chemicals** (only the names are required; their reactions are not part of this course): **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** from old refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays and foams; **halons** from fire extinguishers; **carbon tetrachloride**; **methyl bromide**. The "ozone hole" is a large seasonal thinning of the layer over Antarctica.

**Time-sensitive point (as of 2026):** under the Montreal Protocol (1987) these chemicals have been phased out and the ozone layer is slowly recovering; full recovery is expected only around the middle of the century. Do not confuse the ozone hole (ultraviolet radiation) with global warming (infrared radiation).

key_terms.definition_md: A band of ozone in the stratosphere that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
Chlorofluorocarbons: man-made chemicals that deplete the ozone layer.

sections.heading: 4. Composition of natural water: dissolved oxygen and minerals
sections.body_md:
Natural water carries dissolved substances that living things need.

| Dissolved substance | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Oxygen | Fish and other water animals breathe it; bacteria use it to break down wastes |
| Carbon dioxide | Water plants use it in photosynthesis |
| Calcium and magnesium salts | Bones, teeth and shells |
| Sodium and potassium salts | Balance of body fluids; working of nerves |
| Nitrates and phosphates, in small amounts | Plant nutrients for water plants |

**Dissolved oxygen falls as water gets warmer**, because gases are less soluble in warm water. Approximate textbook values for fresh water in contact with air at sea-level pressure: 14.6 mg per litre at 0 °C; 11.3 mg per litre at 10 °C; 9.1 mg per litre at 20 °C; 7.6 mg per litre at 30 °C; 6.5 mg per litre at 40 °C. Many fish need at least about 5 mg per litre (the value depends on the species). Dissolved oxygen is also reduced when bacteria decay large amounts of waste.

Books differ slightly in the solubility values; the trend (a fall with temperature) is what is examined.

sections.heading: 5. Harmful substances in water: heavy metals, plastics, sewage and pesticides
sections.body_md:
**Toxic heavy metals — Minamata disease.** In the 1950s, a factory at Minamata Bay in Japan discharged waste containing **mercury** into the sea. Microbes changed it into **methylmercury**, which is absorbed by plankton and small fish and **builds up along the food chain**, reaching high amounts in large fish and shellfish. People who ate them developed **damage to the nervous system**: numbness, loss of coordination, and trouble with speech, sight and hearing; in severe cases paralysis, and harm to babies before birth. Other toxic heavy metals include lead, cadmium and arsenic. As of 2026, an international treaty (the Minamata Convention on Mercury, in force since 2017) controls mercury.

**Plastics.** They do not rot, so they stay for hundreds of years; they block drains, are swallowed by or tangle round fish, turtles and birds, and break into tiny pieces. As of 2026, India bans a list of single-use plastic items (in force since 2022).

**Sewage.** Untreated sewage carries disease germs and adds **nitrates and phosphates**. These make algae multiply (algal bloom). When the algae die, bacteria decay them and use up the **dissolved oxygen**, so fish and other animals die.

**Pesticides.** Washed from fields, they poison fish and other animals that were not the target, and may build up along food chains.

Exact figures for fish and mercury limits differ between countries; items use imagined figures.

key_terms.definition_md: A nerve disease caused by eating fish and shellfish contaminated with methylmercury from industrial mercury waste.
Waste water from homes and towns containing human waste, germs and nutrients.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing acid-rain equations that do not balance, or naming **sulphuric** acid for sulphur dioxide plus water (that gives **sulphurous** acid).
- Mixing up the **greenhouse effect** (infrared heat trapped by greenhouse gases) with **ozone depletion** (more ultraviolet radiation).
- Saying that CFCs cause global warming instead of ozone depletion; or that ozone is formed from nitrogen.
- Giving reactions of the ozone-depleting chemicals: only their **names** are needed.
- Saying "mercury" without the food chain in a Minamata answer: it is **methylmercury building up** in fish.
- Forgetting the sequence for sewage: **nutrients, algae, bacteria, low dissolved oxygen, dead fish**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a name, a gas, one effect or one equation.
- 2 marks: two effects, two sources, or an equation with a name.
- 3 marks: three equations, or three points with reasons.
- 10-mark structured question: a diagram or data set followed by parts such as equations, names, causes, effects and a calculation.

questions.stem_md:
A student finds in a reference table the oxygen that fresh water can hold at different temperatures (approximate values, in mg per litre).

| Temperature (°C) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dissolved oxygen (mg per litre) | 14.6 | 11.3 | 9.1 | 7.6 | 6.5 |

(a) State the trend shown by the table and give the reason for it. [2]

(b) Calculate the percentage fall in the dissolved oxygen between 0 °C and 30 °C, to the nearest whole number. [2]

(c) A pond holds 5000 litres of water saturated with oxygen at 30 °C. Calculate the mass of dissolved oxygen in grams. [2]

(d) Why do fish in a warm, shallow pond come to the surface on a still day? [1]

(e) State two reasons why dissolved oxygen, and two reasons why dissolved minerals, are needed by living things in water. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The dissolved oxygen **falls as the temperature rises**, because gases are **less soluble in warm water**.

**(b)** Fall = 14.6 − 7.6 = 7; 7 ÷ 14.6 × 100 = **48%**.

**(c)** 7.6 × 5000 = 38000 mg = **38 g**.

**(d)** The warm water holds **less dissolved oxygen**, so they gasp for air at the surface.

**(e)** Oxygen: fish **breathe** it and bacteria **use it** to break down wastes. Minerals: **calcium and magnesium** build bones, teeth and shells; **sodium and potassium** keep body fluids balanced (or nitrates and phosphates feed plants).

questions.solution_md: Falls with temperature, less soluble gas; 48%; 38 g; less oxygen in warm water; two reasons for oxygen and two for minerals.

questions.stem_md:
A factory beside a coastal bay discharged waste containing mercury into the sea for many years. Fish from the bay were later tested; the mercury found (imagined figures, mg per kg) was 0.04 in plankton, 0.5 in small fish, 2 in large fish and 25 in fish-eating birds. People who ate the fish fell ill.

(a) Name the disease that affected the people and the form of mercury that caused it. [2]

(b) Calculate how many times greater the concentration is in the birds than in the plankton. [2]

(c) Explain what the figures show about how the mercury moves through the food chain. [2]

(d) State two symptoms of the disease. [2]

(e) Suggest two steps that should be taken to prevent a similar disaster. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Minamata disease**, caused by **methylmercury**.

**(b)** 25 ÷ 0.04 = **625 times**.

**(c)** The amount **increases at each step**, so mercury **builds up along the food chain** and is highest in the animals at the top.

**(d)** **Numbness** and **loss of coordination** (or damage to speech, sight or hearing).

**(e)** **Treat factory waste** and stop discharging mercury into water; **test fish** and **warn people** not to eat contaminated fish.

questions.solution_md: Minamata disease and methylmercury; 625 times; builds up along the food chain; numbness and loss of coordination; treat waste, test fish.

marking_scheme.step: Builds up along the food chain

questions.stem_md:
A lake receives untreated sewage, run-off from fertilised fields and plastic waste from a town. After the monsoon the dissolved oxygen falls from 8 mg per litre to 3 mg per litre (imagined readings), and many fish die.

(a) Calculate the percentage fall in dissolved oxygen, to one decimal place. [2]

(b) Explain, in the correct order, how the sewage and run-off lead to the fall in dissolved oxygen. [3]

(c) Name the two nutrients in sewage and fertiliser run-off that cause the algae to grow. [1]

(d) State two ways in which the plastic waste harms the lake and its life. [2]

(e) State two ways in which pesticides washed in from the fields could further harm the lake. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (8 − 3) ÷ 8 × 100 = **62.5%**.

**(b)** **Nitrates and phosphates** make **algae multiply**; the algae die and **bacteria decay them**, using up the **dissolved oxygen**.

**(c)** **Nitrates** and **phosphates**.

**(d)** Plastics **do not rot** and **block drains**; animals **swallow them or get tangled** in them.

**(e)** They **poison fish** and other animals and **build up along the food chain**.

questions.solution_md: 62.5%; nutrients, algae, bacteria, low oxygen; nitrates and phosphates; plastics persist and harm animals; pesticides poison and build up.
